A short tour of a proposed architecture for Iconic CAD, written as lessons: each one adds one idea, with a small hut (one room, about 3.6 x 2.7 m) as the running example. The vocabulary at the end collects every term.

Status: prototyped and tested on a fork (walls, a wall with a window or door, corners, the upper top plate, a floor and the roof framing). Marked ''planned'' where it isn't built yet.

=== The big picture ===

Iconic CAD works in three phases:

* '''Library time''': what ''can'' be built. Contributors write the library; it is checked and compiled ahead of time.
* '''Design time''': what ''you'' build. You pick building blocks from the library and say how they connect; the tool works out the rest.
* '''Build time''': building it. The workshop and the site work from what the design produced: fabrication cards per panel, cut lists, the bill of materials and a build book in build order (''planned'' for the new model).

<pre> LIBRARY TIME                 DESIGN TIME                         BUILD TIME

 modules, systems,            layout: what you                    fabrication cards,
 interfaces                   placed and how it                   cut lists, bill of
 (YAML + JS code)             connects                            materials, build book
       │                            │                                    ▲
       ▼                            ▼                                    │
 library builder ──► library ──► engine ──► model: every part, ──────────┘
                     asset                  joint and issue
                     (one JSON file         (also drives the 3D view)
                     the app loads)</pre>
The app is fully static (no server): catalog modules are compiled when the library is built, and the browser does the rest.

=== Lesson 1: a module is a parametric building block ===

A '''module''' is a kind of building block, such as ''wall panel'' or ''wall panel with opening''. It has '''parameters''' (width, height, stud spacing, lumber, build-up) and code that turns parameter values into '''parts''': each stud, plate, header and sheet, with its size, material and position. That code is the module's '''compiler''' (<code>compile.js</code>).

<pre> wall_panel(width 1200, height 2400, spacing 600, stud 48x148)
   ──►  bottom plate, lower top plate, 3 studs, 1 OSB sheet</pre>

[[File:ic_hut_v2611_module_1200.svg|none|frameless|344px|alt=The wall_panel variant 1200, seen from outside|The wall_panel variant 1200, seen from outside]]
 
[[File:ic_hut_v2611_module_window_10x12.svg|none|frameless|476px|alt=The wall_panel_with_opening variant window_10x12|The wall_panel_with_opening variant window_10x12]]

''Two compiled variants, seen from outside, coloured by role: studs, plates, and for the window the kings, jacks, header, sill and cripples. The OSB is dashed.''

A module knows nothing about where it will stand, or about any country's lumber sizes. That comes next.

=== Lesson 2: a system is a kit ===

A '''system''' is a kit of compatible parts and rules for one way of building: its lumber and sheet catalog, its build-ups (the layers of a wall), its fastening schedule, and its grid. Examples: ''SEH'' (Seed Eco-Home, US sizes) and ''seh_no'' (SEH adapted to Norway: metric, studs at 600 mm).

A module and a system meet in a '''variant''': a named, fixed set of parameter values for that module in that system.

<pre>                                 system: seh_no (48x148, OSB 12, c/c 600, ...)
 module: wall_panel              ──►   variants &quot;1200&quot;, &quot;600&quot; (width), height 2400
 module: wall_panel_with_opening ──►   variants &quot;window_10x12&quot;, &quot;door_10x20&quot;</pre>
Users place variants, not raw parameters, so every placed block is a standard, checked panel, and identical panels can be built in a batch. A module is in a system if the system has variants for it; that list is the system's palette in the app.

A '''build-up''' belongs to the system, e.g. ''exterior wall'': OSB on the outside (fitted in the workshop), then wind barrier, battens and cladding (fitted on site). Each layer says whether it is part of the panel or added on site.

=== Lesson 3: ports and interfaces say how blocks connect ===

Each module has '''ports''': named connection points, such as a wall's <code>left</code> and <code>right</code> ends. An '''interface''' is an agreement between two '''roles''' about how two ports meet. The wall corner has two roles: ''through'' (the wall that runs to the outer corner) and ''butt'' (the wall that stops against it).

A port fills a role if its module says it can, and two ports connect if they fill the two roles of one interface.

The interface does two jobs:

# '''Places''' the modules: a fixed rule (here: turn 90 degrees, offset by the wall's framing depth).
# Says what each role must offer, e.g. the through wall must expose its end stud and outer sheet.

''How'' the corner is actually built is an '''implementation''' of the interface (the trade calls it a construction detail). For seh_no the corner's implementation is the ''California corner'': a turned stud in the through wall gives both linings something to nail to. Implementations add parts (the turned stud, a strip of OSB) and choose nothing about position, so switching to another corner detail never moves a wall.

[[File:ic_hut_v2611_corner_plan.svg|none|frameless|680px|alt=The hut's south-east corner in plan|The hut's south-east corner in plan]]

''The hut's south-east corner, cut at 1000 mm. S3 runs through and E1 butts against it; the wall_corner interface placed them. The orange parts come from the implementation and are fitted on site.''

=== Lesson 4: a design is a list of choices, not coordinates ===

A '''layout''' stores what you decided: the placed blocks ('''entities'''), how they connect ('''connections''') and one '''anchor''' that pins the first block in place. No coordinates.

<pre>"entities": [
  {"id": "S1", "module": "wall_panel", "variant": "1200"},
  {"id": "S2", "module": "wall_panel_with_opening", "variant": "window_10x12"},
  {"id": "S3", "module": "wall_panel", "variant": "600"},
  {"id": "E1", "module": "wall_panel", "variant": "1200"}
],
"connections": [
  {"id": "c_s12", "interface": "wall_inline", "a": "S1.right", "b": "S2.left"},
  {"id": "c_s23", "interface": "wall_inline", "a": "S2.right", "b": "S3.left"},
  {"id": "c_se",  "interface": "wall_corner", "through": "S3.right", "butt": "E1.left"}
]</pre>
The hut is ten panels joined by four corners: the window in the south wall (1200 + window + 600), the door in the west wall (600 + door), and plain 1200 panels to the north and east. Each wall keeps a solid stretch at least 600 wide for bracing.

[[File:ic_hut_v2611_layout_graph.svg|none|frameless|720px|alt=The hut's layout as a graph, and the plan the engine works out|The hut's layout as a graph, and the plan the engine works out]]

''Left: all the layout stores. Right: the positions the engine derives from it (Lesson 5).''

Because the layout keeps the topology rather than positions, it survives changes in size, and could be converted to another system (''planned'').

=== Lesson 5: the engine turns a layout into a model ===

The '''engine''' walks the connections from the anchor, placing each entity with the interface's rule, and assembles the finished parts into the '''model''': every entity's position, every part, every joint, and every '''issue''' (a problem found by a check, such as walls that don't close into a loop). It always produces a model, so a half-finished design can still be shown with its problems marked.

Everything downstream (3D view, bill of materials, build book) reads the model; nothing recomputes framing on its own.

[[File:ic_hut_v2611_assembly.gif|none|frameless|720px|alt=The engine building the hut's model, step by step|The engine building the hut's model, step by step]]

''The engine building the hut's model: the anchor, then each panel as the walk reaches it through a connection (the corner parts come once both walls are in), then the derived upper top plate, floor and roof (Lesson 6).''

=== Lesson 6: derived modules fill in what follows from the whole design ===

Some things can't belong to a single panel because they depend on the neighbours:

* the '''upper top plate''', which laps the corners and bridges the joints between panels;
* the '''floor''', whose size and joists follow the walls standing on it;
* the '''roof''', whose rafters sit on the walls' top plates;
* later the '''foundation'''.

These come from '''derived modules'''. You don't place them: the layout lists the ones the design uses, with their parameters, and the engine runs them in order once the walls close:

<pre>"derive": [
  {"module": "storey"},
  {"module": "roof", "after": ["storey"], "parameters": {"pitch": 27, "ridge": "east_west", "eaves": 400, "gables": 300}}
]</pre>
<pre> storey  (the walls on one level)
   ├── wall_line  × 4   one per straight run of panels: the upper top plate,
   │                    in pieces of at most 2400, joints 600 from panel joints
   └── floor            outline = the walls' framing; sill, rims, joists c/c 600,
                        blocking under the gable walls' studs, chipboard on top
 roof   (after the storey)
                        rafters c/c 600 in birdsmouths on the top plates, a
                        ridge board, ceiling joists that tie the rafters' feet,
                        gable studs, a ladder at each gable for the overhang</pre>
Each module sees the model so far, plus a summary from the modules it comes after: the storey tells the roof where its plates are and which walls face which way. If the roof fails, the walls and the floor stay in the model, with the problem reported. A derived module's parameters come from two places, like a catalog module's: the system fixes some (the lumber, the spacing), and the layout gives the rest (the pitch, which way the ridge runs, the overhang).

The ordinary modules are called '''catalog modules''': they are compiled ahead of time and placed by the user. A derived module's code (<code>derive.js</code>) gets the design so far as input, such as the placed walls, so it runs in the browser each time the design changes rather than ahead of time.

Parts don't have to be square to the building: a rafter is a box in its own tilted frame, with plane cuts (at the ridge and the tail) and a notch where it sits on the plate (the birdsmouth).

[[File:ic_hut_v2611_module_wall_lines.svg|none|frameless|720px|alt=The four wall lines with the upper top plate|The four wall lines with the upper top plate]]

''The four wall lines from outside. The upper top plate (dark orange) laps the corners, and its joints stay 600 mm from the joints between panels.''

[[File:ic_hut_v2611_module_floor.svg|none|frameless|720px|alt=The derived floor in plan|The derived floor in plan]]

''The floor in plan, derived from the walls: a sill all round, rims, joists at 600, and blocking (orange) under the studs of the gable walls (grey).''

[[File:ic_hut_v2611_roof_framing.svg|none|frameless|720px|alt=The roof framing on the upper top plates|The roof framing on the upper top plates]]

''The roof at 27°: rafters in birdsmouths on the upper top plates, the ridge board, a ceiling joist beside each rafter between the gables, gable studs under the end rafters, and at each gable a ladder (a fly rafter and lookouts) for the 300 mm overhang.''

[[File:ic_hut_v2611_storey_framing.svg|none|frameless|720px|alt=The hut's framing without sheets|The hut's framing without sheets]]

''The hut's framing, with the sheets hidden.''

=== Lesson 7: parts are held together by joints ===

Inside a module, and where modules meet, two parts held together form a '''joint''', of a named '''joint type''' such as <code>stud_to_plate</code> or <code>sheathing_to_framing</code>. The joint type says ''what'' is joined; the system's '''fastening schedule''' says ''how'': which nail or screw, and how many or how far apart.

<pre> joint type  stud_to_plate
 seh_no      2 nails 2.8x95, toe-nailed from the stud</pre>
So the same design gets nails in one system and screws in another, and fastener counts come out of the model instead of being typed in by hand.

Joints mirror interfaces one level down:

{| class="wikitable"
|-
!
! Between modules
! Between parts
|-
| The contract
| interface (<code>wall_corner</code>)
| joint type (<code>stud_to_plate</code>)
|-
| How, per system
| implementation (<code>california</code>)
| fastening schedule entry
|-
| One occurrence
| connection (chosen by the user)
| joint (computed)
|}

=== Lesson 8: library time, design time, build time ===

{| class="wikitable"
|-
!
! Library time
! Design time
! Build time
|-
| Who
| contributors and CI
| the person designing
| the builders, in the workshop and on site
|-
| Runs
| the library builder (Node)
| the editor and the engine (browser)
| nothing new: they read the outputs
|-
| Does
| checks the library, compiles every variant, applies placement rules and builds every corner pair in advance
| places entities, runs derived modules, checks the design
| fabricates panels (identical variants in a batch), then erects them and fits the site parts in build order
|-
| Output
| the '''library asset''' (one JSON file)
| the '''model''', and the outputs read from it
| the building
|}

Library code (module compilers, implementations, derived modules) is plain JavaScript, so the same code runs in Node at library time and in the browser at design time, with no server.

=== Lesson 9: code profiles check the design (''planned'') ===

A '''code profile''' is a building code with its edition, such as Eurocode 5 (EN 1995-1-1) with a national annex, or IRC 2021. It is chosen separately from the system, because one system can be used under several codes. It supplies loads and checks (spans, bracing, snow load) against the project's '''site values''' (snow load, wind, climate). The rule: ''the system supplies, the code checks''.

=== The library on disk ===

<pre>library/
  modules/wall_panel/
    schema.yaml            parameters and ports, independent of any system
    compile.js             turns parameters into parts (derive.js for a derived module)
    systems/seh_no.yaml    this module's variants in seh_no
  interfaces/wall_corner/
    interface.yaml         roles, placement rule, checks
    implementations/california.js
    systems/seh_no.yaml    which implementation seh_no uses
  systems/seh_no/
    system.yaml            catalog, build-ups, fastening schedule</pre>
Adding a module to a system, or a whole new system, only adds files; a contributor's change is typically one folder and one pull request.

=== Toolchain ===

The toolchain is a few '''components''', each a separately runnable program, connected by '''artifacts''' (files). Each component works in '''passes''', steps that hand their result to the next in memory. A component can be replaced without touching the others as long as it reads and writes the same artifacts.

<pre> library source ──► library builder ──► library asset ──┐
                                                         ├──► engine ──► model ──► consumers ──► outputs
                         layout (from the editor) ───────┘</pre>
{| class="wikitable"
|-
! Component
! Reads
! Writes
! Passes
|-
| '''Library builder''' (<code>scripts/build_library.mjs</code>, Node)
| library source
| library asset
| load, validate, resolve parameters against the system, compile variants, place and build implementations for every port pair, export
|-
| '''Editor''' (the app's UI, browser)
| library asset
| layout
|
|-
| '''Engine''' (browser, or Node for tests and the command line)
| layout, library asset
| model
| load, check, place, close loops, assemble, run derived modules, summarise
|-
| '''Consumers''' (3D view, plan, bill of materials, build book, FreeCAD export)
| model
| outputs
|
|}

{| class="wikitable"
|-
! Artifact
! What it is
! Example
|-
| '''Library source'''
| The library as contributors write it: YAML for schemas, systems and interfaces; JavaScript for module code and implementations
| <code>library/</code>
|-
| '''Library asset'''
| The compiled library: every variant's parts, every port pair's placement and implementation, derived modules' parameters
| <code>web/assets/library.json</code>
|-
| '''Layout'''
| A design: entities, connections, anchor, which derived module to run
| <code>hut.json</code>
|-
| '''Model'''
| Positions, parts, joints and issues
| <code>hut.model.json</code>
|-
| '''Outputs'''
| What people use
| SVG drawings, CSV lists, <code>.FCStd</code>, PDF build book
|}

Generated artifacts are only changed by regenerating them. The editor reads only the library asset, which keeps the app independent of how the library is written.

Checks split by phase: anything about one module, variant or interface runs in the library builder (parameter ranges, catalog references, whether two variants can meet); anything about a whole design runs in the engine (loops close, no port used twice, and later the code profile's checks).
